utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. If I am looking -- you are standing on both sides. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good day to you, Mr. President. The Defence wishes to raise some issues with regard to what is called WY, or is it vice versa? It is a request by the Prosecution of May 24th, 1992 -- 2002. The Defence would like to respond. The Defence would like to remind the Chamber that, as far as it knows, the Prosecution has never asked for the possibility to add the two witnesses to its list. So now we are in a situation where the Prosecution -- I don't think I have seen this, but the Prosecution is asking for protective measures for two new witnesses, and as far as I know, we haven't known -- we don't know about these two names. I may be wrong. We would like to respond in written form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...written response given.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we could do it quite quickly. During this week, we can respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would highly appreciate it if you would do it this week. Since you are mentioning this week yourself, we only too gladly accept that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could do it later, but we could do it this week also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, yes, first of all, I will respond to my friend's concern. Indeed, both of those witnesses were on the original witness list filed by the Prosecution pursuant to Rule 65 ter of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. They were referred to by their pseudonyms, so they are not new witnesses. Witness W is being called next Tuesday so, naturally, it is essential that a decision be made as soon as possible. Mr. President, there are a few other matters that I would like to raise from the Prosecution side. Firstly, in relation to the course of today's proceedings and the proceedings for tomorrow and Friday. Mr. President, I am not aware of any notice problem that the Defence might have in relation to their preparedness to cross-examine Mr. O'Keefe. I think that we have complied with all of the timetables. I would therefore respectfully submit that it would be appropriate for that witness to be dealt with today. I anticipate that he could be finished today entirely. I am aware that my friend has sought an adjournment in order to prepare himself, the Defence to prepare itself, for cross-examination of Mr. Thomas. The Prosecution would also benefit from a short adjournment before he is taken in chief. Might I, therefore, respectfully submit that once O'Keeffe is finished today, if that is the course that the Trial Chamber takes, we then adjourn until tomorrow afternoon, at which time the Prosecution would deal with Thomas in chief. If, by the end of his evidence in chief, the Defence reasonably requires further time, then that could be dealt with at that point. I think there are some documents or portions of documents which have not been served by the Prosecution on the Defence pursuant to the timetable. So the Prosecution accepts that there may be a problem with Thomas. Mr. President, as I have said, over the last two days, we have done what we could to fill any gap this week with other witnesses, and we have been unable to do that. Whilst the witness O'Keeffe is likely to be relatively brief in chief, and therefore in cross-examination I expect that the witness Thomas will take some time, therefore, any shortfall in the timetable this week may not be as great as I earlier feared. Mr. President, yesterday, on other matter, I indicated that the Prosecution intends to not call the witness Southwell, or "Southall" as it is properly pronounced. There are some exhibits which were to be tendered through him. We will seek to add some of those exhibits to a future witness for the relevant period. Mr. President, having dropped that witness, the Prosecution would like to retrieve one of the witnesses which I indicated a week ago we would drop; that is Pierce Tucker. I hasten to add that his evidence will be short. There are three or four relevant parts. There is a problem also with the Prosecution timetable for Wednesday and Thursday next week. I don't know that it is necessary for me to explain the detail of those problems. Perhaps it is sufficient to say that international witnesses, by their nature, are not easily marshalled. I, therefore, have in mind, if it is acceptable to the Trial Chamber, to call Pierce Tucker next Wednesday and to ensure that the Defence has by tomorrow morning a copy of his statement with the relevant parts translated, and in addition, the relevant parts of his statement indicated by me to the Defence as being the parts about which he will give evidence. Mr. Tucker has given a lengthy statement recently to the Office of the Prosecutor. Much of it has nothing to do with Sarajevo. To give an example, I think there are some ten pages which relate to events in Srebrenica. Therefore, we would exercise maximum flexibility to ensure that the Defence is not prejudiced by this proposed timetable. If, however, Mr. President and Your Honours, you think that that would be unfair to the Defence, then at this stage we would simply seek to retrieve him onto the witness list and call him at a later point. There may be, as I have said, a problem mid next week. We propose to call David Harland on Thursday. Again, there are some difficulties, but we expect that we will be able to produce him on Thursday to give evidence. I do not expect any problem with the witness we have allocated for Friday, nor do I expect any problem with Mr. Mole for Monday and Witness W on Tuesday. Mr. Mole on Monday may be a lengthy witness, and if we have not finished his evidence by Tuesday morning, I would seek to interpose Witness W. He is only available to give evidence on that day, or at least I should say, given his commitments, he and the relevant government would appreciate him leaving by that day, the end of that day. That, Mr. President, is the situation. I do apologise for these changes. I assure you that the changes do not reflect any lack of diligence on the part of the Prosecution, rather, if I could use the vernacular, it is the nature of the beast. International witnesses by definition are difficult to organise. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you may respond, but I would say rather briefly at this very moment because we first, of course, will have to see what happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. It will be very brief. I believe the Prosecution has been showing flexibility, but things seem to be inversed. The calendars are totally changed, witnesses that we have known nothing about are being proposed, and this is not acceptable. It is not possible for the Defence within a period of few hours to prepare for cross-examination of witnesses in such a short period of time we don't have time to reflect on these matters. And we don't have the possibility of contacting the accused on these matters. If this is not a violation of the rights of the Defence, I don't know what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, we will have to consider the -- yes, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour. The Defence would like to inform the Chamber that while preparing the cross-examination of Mr. O'Keeffe, we didn't have time enough to have the disclosed 23 documents, to inform General Galic about them, and this is a problem which the Defence is faced with. We expect that we might be able to ask for your leave to have Mr. O'Keeffe re-invited to come or to have a shorter period of time to have -- to acquaint the General with the information. We have gone through the material this morning. We have come to the trial now and we were not able to show the General these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that you had considerable problems in preparing, especially in conferring with your client. Would Mr. O'Keeffe still be available tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Wouldn't it be a wise thing that decisions to be taken at this very moment is perhaps not the best thing to do but at least, during the examination-in-chief of Mr. O'Keeffe, that you give, in one way or the other, just an indication to the Bench when you deal with those documents that had only been recently provided to the Defence, that the Chamber is better able to assess to what extent the examination-in-chief deals with these documents. Of course, we haven't seen them, but that we don't have to guess later on which was new and what was already known before to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, firstly, Mr. O'Keeffe will be taken by Mr. Mundis, but let me say this: There are no fresh documents with Mr. O'Keeffe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but there are documents which were not translated at an earlier date and of which the Defence has told us that they were not able to discuss them with General Galic. So we would like to know, for example, in order to know what portion of the evidence is related to these documents, so that we have at least a clue and that we will, in a later stage, better be able to take into consideration all circumstances in all details. Yes. Then, Mr. Mundis --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might I be excused, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Prosecution calls Mr. Donough O'Keeffe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Usher, would you please assist in escorting Mr. O'Keeffe into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. O'Keeffe, may I take it that you can hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. O'Keeffe, before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of the declaration will be handed out to you now by the usher. May I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated, Mr. O'Keeffe. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mr. O'Keeffe, counsel for the Prosecution will start to examine you. Mr. Mundis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: For the record, sir, can you please state your full name and spell your last name, please.

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: My full name is Donough O'Keeffe. My last name is spelled Oscar Kilo Echo Echo Foxtrot Foxtrot Echo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. O'Keeffe, are you a currently a member of the Irish Defence Forces?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What is your current rank?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: My rank is commandant, which would be the equivalent of major in other armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, how long have you been a member of the Irish Defence Forces?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: For 38 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What branch or specialization in the Irish Defence Forces are you a member of?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I am a member of the Infantry Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time, sir, when you were posted to the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was your assignment in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Senior Military observer, Sector Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately, what date did you report for duty in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Approximately the 16th of March, but I am not sure. I am not sure of that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And which year was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: For how long did you remain senior military observer in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Approximately three and a half months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate date that you departed Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: It was after the 16th of June. I know it was sometime just after the 16th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall whom you relieved as senior military observer in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes. Jim Cutler, a New Zealander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, when you departed Sarajevo in June 1993, who was your successor?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Jorma Kukkola was my successor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What were your primary duties and responsibilities as Senior Military Observer, Sector Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: The security of my UNMOs was paramount. My mission there was to monitor the ceasefire, to monitor the heavy weapons around Sarajevo, to assist in the humanitarian convoys, and to report as a military observer to my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In what form did the reports to your military superiors take?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Each day, we wrote a report at the end of the day. Also -- sorry. This report went to the senior military observer of UNPROFOR and it also went to the sector commander of UNPROFOR in Sarajevo Sector. We also submitted logs - I mean daily logsheets - of events that happened during the day to the sector commander of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The information that was contained in the daily reports, how did you receive that information?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I had military observers on what we called the Lima side which was monitors on the Serbian side of the front line. We had Papa observers inside the city. These observers made their reports during the day. These reports were compiled into a full report by my staff and we would submit this report at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the time you were senior military observer in Sarajevo, do you recall approximately how many UN military observers you had on the Papa side?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I am not sure. The total number of UNMOs varied from approximately 40 to 70 during my time. As far as I recollect, we had less than half of the UNMOs in the Papa side. So, at times, it could be between 10 to 15 UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On the Papa side?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With the remainder on the Lima side?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Correct. Except those -- except the observers working at the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall during the time that you were senior military observer in Sarajevo, how many Papa observation posts were in existence?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I think approximately five. I am not sure how many exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How many observation posts on the Lima side?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there were more -- more than the Papa side, but I could not say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did your responsibilities as senior military observer include lodging formal protests or complaints with either of the warring sides?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes. We, on the Papa side and on the Lima side, they -- both the senior observers, they both lodged complaints. I, at the beginning, lodged complaints, but very shortly after I taking over, all formal protests had to be made through sector commander Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the time you were in Sarajevo, who was the sector commander Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Colonel Valentin, a French officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate date or time period in which the sector commander Sarajevo assumed responsibility for making formal protests?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I could not -- I could not be sure, but I think approximately early April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Prior to that period, did you personally make any formal protests to the Bosnian Serb army side?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes. I personally protested against the targeting of one of our observation posts on the Papa side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate date that you made this protest?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: It was during April. I don't know -- I don't know. I couldn't say which date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall whom you met with on the Bosnian Serb army side when making this protest?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I met Colonel Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was that the first instance that you met with him?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When was the first time you met with Colonel Galic?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: When I was taking over from Colonel Cutler, he was giving me a briefing of the situation in Sarajevo, and I attended a meeting with him in Colonel Galic's office during my first week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where was this office located?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: In the barracks in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was this also an opportunity for Colonel Cutler to introduce you to the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you take part in any of the substantive discussions at that time?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: You mean, during the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I was there during the meeting, all the time during the meeting, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you personally say anything to Colonel Galic at that time?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes. I introduced myself as an officer of the Defence Forces of Ireland. I explained to him that I had been sent here by my government to assist him in their crisis. I assured him that I would be totally impartial during my time as senior military observer and I expected him to treat the military observers with the respect that was due to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how long this meeting lasted?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: No, I don't. I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did the situation with respect to the observation post that was the subject of this discussion improve following this meeting?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Can you phrase that again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Certainly. Let me backtrack one question. Do you recall which observation post was the subject matter of the discussion with Colonel Galic on that day?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: It was Papa 5, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Following the meeting with Colonel Galic, did the situation with respect to Papa 5 improve?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: No. Because during my time, Papa 5 was targeted again, and I witnessed the explosion when I witnessed the explosion at our observation post from a distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate time period that you witnessed an explosion at Papa 5?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I couldn't say which day at this time. Sometime in April, is the best I could say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what steps did you take after you witnessed this explosion?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: You mean, what progress I made?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I arranged a meeting with Colonel Galic as soon as possible after this incident, and I protested to him about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall during this second meeting with Colonel Galic, what you told him?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I told him that we were trying to find another position where we could have an observation post, but I was not successful in finding a position up to that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you discussed any other issues with Colonel Galic at that meeting, other than Papa 5?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I don't recall discussing anything in particular, but I would have made the normal protest about the issues going on at the time, if I had a meeting with Colonel Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say, "the normal protest about the issues going on at the time," what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I would be referring to the treatment of my UNMOs, the sniping that has been carried out and the indiscriminate shelling, and the stopping of humanitarian aid coming into the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "the indiscriminate shelling"?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I considered a lot of the shelling was not -- was not targeted on military targets, that shells were landing in all areas. And I could not understand these to be military targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Upon what did you base this conclusion that you held?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Basically, from my previous experiences with UN missions, and I could see no military purpose in a lot of the shelling that has been carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you convey these concerns to General Galic?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what, if anything, he said to you in response?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Having reflected a bit, I have to intervene because of the interpretation. According to the interpretation with regard to the -- to most of the shelling, this is not what the witness said. He didn't say "for the most part," he said "numerous shelling." I think it is necessary to distinguish this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly proper attention will be taken in respect of your observation. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Commandant O'Keeffe, let me repeat the question: Do you recall what, if anything, he said to you in response?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I only remember one particular phrase that comes to mind, and he said that he was going to make this area safe for his children's children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than these two instances that you have described for us, did you ever meet with General Galic on any other occasion?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot say exactly how many times, but when I was visiting the UNMOs on the Lima side, I would always call to the UNMO headquarters which was situated in Lukavica barracks. And I almost every time asked to see Colonel Galic or the gentleman that was known as the liaison officer during my visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You said you cannot say exactly how many times. Are you in a position to say approximately how many times you saw Colonel Galic?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I think maybe eight or nine times, but I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to characterise these visits with General Galic or Colonel Galic at that time as being examples of military courtesy or protocol?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Affirmative, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall on any of these eight or nine occasions if you had any substantive discussions with him?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I cannot recall these meetings as such and what was stated at these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to characterise these brief meetings as simply an opportunity for you to inform the corps commander that you were in his headquarters building?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Not really. I would have -- I would have discussed -- I would have discussed certain ongoing issues with him. It would be normal for me to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you give us some examples of these ongoing issues?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Well, I don't -- I don't recall speaking to him about any particular issues during these meetings as such. So I would be wrong to say -- I couldn't -- sorry. I can't say that I discussed any particular issue with him during these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many times you met with the liaison officer at Lukavica barracks?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I would think approximately eight or nine times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of the liaison officer that you met with at Lukavica barracks?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what issues you discussed with the liaison officer at Lukavica barracks?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: No, I don't recall. I am not good with names and -- because I don't even recall the senior military observer's name who was at Lukavica barracks at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say, "the senior military observer at Lukavica," do you mean the liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes. He was the liaison officer and also the senior military observer on the Lima side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This would be the senior UNMO on the Lima side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Commandant O'Keeffe, upon your arrival or shortly after your arrival in Sarajevo, did you have the opportunity to travel around the various Lima observation posts?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: In my first week, I travelled all -- to all the Lima positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was this part of an orientation programme to familiarise you with the Lima OPs?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the time you were on this orientation tour, did you have the opportunity to visit any of the Bosnian Serb army gun locations?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes, I visited some locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many locations you visited?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Maybe two or three. I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the orientation tour while you were at these gun locations, did you see any of the Bosnian Serb army guns being fired?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes. I witnessed at one position a large -- a large amount of rounds being fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate location of these gun positions?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: No, I couldn't -- I couldn't say where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many rounds were fired?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: My impression is that up to about 500 rounds were fired during the time when I was at this position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall witnessing or seeing where those rounds were landing?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: No, I couldn't see from the gun position where they landed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the details, any other details, about what you saw on that day at that location?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: No, I don't recall any other details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall at any other time during your tenure in Sarajevo, being at a Bosnian Serb army gun line when guns were being fired?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes. I was visiting one Lima position on a certain day and I was brought to one or the gun positions, and they were firing from that position on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many rounds were fired on that day?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I think roughly around 200 rounds is what I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall being at Bosnian Serb army gun lines at any time when a gunner was being trained?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes. The incident I am referring to, I was told that one of the gunners was being trained that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What do you recall that you witnessed with respect to that incident?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I recall, in particular, the amount of ammunition that was placed near the guns at the site because it amazed me that there was so much ammunition out in the open, ready to be fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how much ammunition you saw?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I couldn't put a figure on it, but I can picture a heap of ammunition, which would be approximately, maybe, 6 metres long by 4 metres high -- sorry, 3 metres high. 6 metres long, 3 metres high and 3 metres wide, which to me was a lot of ammunition at the gun site.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you have any discussions with any of the UNMOs with respect to the amounts of ammunition near Bosnian Serb army guns?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: My lasting impression was that there was absolutely no problem at any time about the amount of ammunition that was available to all the weapons on the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Commandant O'Keeffe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Prosecution has no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. I never heard you anywhere indicate that you were referring to any newly translated. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you, under the present circumstances, tell us whether you are or whether you would be within a reasonable time, ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have to tell you the truth. I don't know. I don't know because we haven't had the time to have a look at the documents and to confer with General Galic. As a result, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it be of any assistance to have a break at this moment, perhaps a break which lasts a bit longer than usual, so that you would have an opportunity to discuss the present situation with General Galic and then inform the Chamber where we are?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I thank you for that. We also respect this witness who shouldn't be kept here for too long. I think an extended pause would be interesting, but I don't think that it would suffice for us to see what all the problems are. But if we could advance a bit and take this break and perhaps start with cross-examining this witness, and we have seen in addition that he can't remember much, why not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would prefer that you would refrain from commenting on --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, before we break, if in fact we are going to break at this time, if the Chamber is able to provide any clarification with respect to the next witness, the Prosecution would be grateful so that we could notify the Victims and Witnesses Unit in respect to whether that witness will be testifying today or tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we were informed that the next witness would be Mr. Thomas, but that the Prosecution would need further time to prepare the examination-in-chief. So perhaps I should ask a similar question to you, that during the break, to consider whether you would be prepared to start the examination of the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: As you correctly stated, Mr. President, Mr. Thomas is the next witness. We would be prepared to start with him in examination-in-chief tomorrow at 1415 hours, the regularly scheduled time tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That means that you would have no other witness for today?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, it highly depends on what happens in the rest of this afternoon. It is very difficult for us at this moment to give you an indication. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, should any special measures be taken in order to make the full time for the next break available to you to confer with General Galic or is that just a matter of routine?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you mean by "special measures," Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether -- for whatever security reasons or organisational reasons, if you would adjourn now, would you be in a position to confer with General Galic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the extent that I will be permitted to take my computer to the room, and documents, then I will do so, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any security issues in taking computers to the conference room? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. We will adjourn until 4.00. If there is any specific problem in that respect, the Chamber would like to be informed about it right away. So not after the break but even during the break, whenever it comes up, so that we can see whether there will be a solution for that. But let me just first listen to the always wise words of Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am informed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that taking your computer to the room where you confer with General Galic will not be a problem. And the documents, I take it that is similar, yes. Then we will adjourn until 4.00. --- Break taken at 3.16 p.m

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you inform the Chamber about the position the Defence takes at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Mr. President. Defence counsel has used the time of this break, and we thank you for that, and we have tried to confer with General Galic and we arrived at the following conclusion: What we will do, if the Trial Chamber allows us to do so, is to cross-examine in tandem, so both of us will examine this witness. And we would like to point out that if it seems to be necessary at the end of this hearing to call the witness back, we will ask the permission of the Trial Chamber to do so. But, for the moment, we will do everything we can on the basis of the few extra minutes we have had in order to prepare this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before giving you the opportunity to do so, Mr. Mundis, may I ask you, since at the beginning of the examination-in-chief I asked the Prosecution to indicate where it would refer to these, well, let's say, newly translated lines: When did you inform the Defence that you would not do so or was it just did it come up in your mind during examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, are you referring to using the documents that had been listed as exhibits?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but also those documents provided to the Defence indicating which lines you might confront the witness with and giving a translation of these lines. That is what I understood it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The decision was taken during the course of the examination not to confront the witness with any of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because if you would have taken the decision prior to starting the examination-in-chief, of course, it would have been proper to inform the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because they are, I take it, very much concentrating on these documents and spending a lot of time on it. It is a bit of unlucky course of events first providing them with, well, at least an indication of what you might use. I mean, otherwise, you might not have taken the effort to have those parts translated. I appreciate that it was in the mind of the Prosecution to assist the Defence. But they are shaken from one point to another, and that takes a lot of energy in preparing for cross-examination as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. President. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I just wanted to make that clear to start with so that, with a clear and open mind, we could now ask the usher again to -- ask the usher to -- yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. In order to be -- to respect the practice of the parties, we made use of this witness and had a cassette viewed. This decision was taken in the cell, if I may say so, after what we were able to decide. We have a copy here, one for the Prosecution, one for the Registry, of course, but we weren't able to inform of this 24 hours in advance. We were put in a spot, in a certain sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You heard, Mr. Mundis, that Mr. Piletta-Zanin just announced that they will have a videocassette, that is what I understand, being shown to the witness, that they will have a videocassette shown to the witness and that they decided only during this break to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I understand what Mr. Piletta-Zanin has said, Mr. President. I certainly have not seen this tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Shall we follow the same procedure, that is, that we discuss the issues at the very moment where we know exactly what the issue is about. If it is a videotape that you are viewing five times a week, it might not be necessary to ask for further preparation time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If I could, Mr. President, if this is a tape that has been disclosed by the Prosecution, if my learned friend could so indicate, perhaps we could then --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. It is a personal -- personal tape, a personal production, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has it been disclosed to the Prosecution before?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, since we thought we would use it for another witness, but given what we have found out, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't there is reciprocal disclosure among the parties which would entitle the Prosecution to inspect? So it is on the list of those objects to be inspected by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, because we never tendered it. We have never offered it to the Prosecution until now. The decision was just taken. We have these documents in another cupboard, and we suddenly took this decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just try to make it clear. Is it not the case that the reciprocal of this disclosure has been triggered by the Defence itself under Rule - I see that my colleague is just trying to find the rule of reciprocal disclosure - under Rule 67. If the Defence makes a request pursuant to Rule 66(B), and as far as I understand such a request has been made, but please correct me if I am wrong, then the Prosecutor shall be entitled to inspect any books, documents, photographs or tangible objects which are within the custody or control of the Defence and which it intends to use as evidence. You say you only now decided -- when did you decide that, during the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we decided it during the break, given our conference with General Galic. So it served a purpose, that meeting. And we didn't have the time to prepare it with the appropriate numbers and things. It is something that we had in one of our cupboards. What we can do is provide the Prosecution with a cassette this evening and then ask the witness to come back, but I don't think we will gain much time. Given the urgency of the matter, we had to act in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think my learned colleague has answered the question that you have asked. There is a broader issue here, and I don't seek to derail these proceedings. I appreciate that Mr. O'Keeffe is waiting. Could I simply identify an issue, and at some later stage in the week, having identified it, there could be further discussion of this issue. Approximately two weeks ago, I asked the Defence, in relation to this Rule, if they had provided us with all of the material which they were required to do under this Rule. And I was informed that I would be advised in due course. I am yet to receive an answer. Secondly, I specifically asked the Defence if I could inspect the originals of the various orders and of the documents which appear to have come from the archives of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, and I was told I would be advised about that. We still have not heard from the Defence in relation to this tape, why it has not been disclosed to us. Mr. President, perhaps at some appropriate time when we run out of witnesses, either later today or tomorrow or Friday, we could revisit this issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps it is not the proper time at this very moment. I notice that request for inspection of originals have been made several times by the Defence. I now hear that the Prosecution is asking originals from the Defence. I think this is not a proper moment to discuss that in rather general terms. I suggest that we first proceed with the cross-examination of Mr. O'Keeffe and that the Prosecution will have an opportunity on -- to see what the Prosecution would need after we have seen the video. I do understand that it is new video. Is it in a form to which it can be played? And you have copies for everyone?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have the original here for the usher and we have the same for the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have a copy for the Prosecution already?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was very fortunate that, when we took the decision, there was at least copies for the other party as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, one remaining matter. Might Mr. Thomas be excused for the remainder of this session? We could contact the Victims and Witnesses Unit if you thought it appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was informed by Mr. Mundis that he could not be examined today. So we accepted that, perhaps not specifically, but we did not oppose against the observation of Mr. Mundis that he would not be available to testify today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the video, do you want portions to be played or do you want the whole video to be played? The video you prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I was talking with my colleague. It is rather brief in duration, 2 minutes 25, so we will show it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is not more than two minutes, okay. Perhaps you already give it to the booth that they could already put it on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will give it -- I will provide the booth with it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I see that Madam Registrar is now performing all essential functions in this courtroom. We will wait until the usher returns and then ask him to escort Mr. O'Keeffe in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Usher. Mr. O'Keeffe, we apologise for having you to wait so long.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No problem, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, as usual, lawyers have their procedural issues they want to discuss. Mr. O'Keeffe, you will now be cross-examined, at least, cross-examining will start and you will be cross-examined by counsel for the Defence. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Commandant, good day.

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Commandant, I will ask questions in French. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: As we say in our profession, five-to-five?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I don't understand "five-to-five."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: That usually means loud and clear, perfectly. Can you hear me loud and clear?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Just to be clear. Commandant, have you made a written statement to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Would you tell us what the date was?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I don't remember. It was about three years ago when I made the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I would like to provide you with the text of your statement and I would like you to confirm simply that this is your signature on the document, if you please. If the Chamber allows me.

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Commandant, would you agree with me that your statement was made on May 12, 13, and 14, 1998?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: If that is the date that the -- that is written on the document that I signed, then I accept that as the correct date.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Good. Sir, you spent a certain amount of time in Sarajevo. Do you know whether it was usual for the observers, the military observers, to devote more than three or four months of time in that town?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: It was the normal practice at -- before I went to Sarajevo for the UNMOs to have a rotation system every three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: In other words, Colonel, you are saying that, as a rule, the MOs, military observers of the United Nations, did not stay longer than three or four months in Sarajevo? As a rule, in principle, that is what I am trying to ask you.

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Sir, is it correct to say that for reasons of protocol, the rule in use was that one would address a colonel as a colonel and a major as a major and a general -- to a general of equal rank; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I am not sure what you are getting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I shall rephrase my question. When there was discussion, for instance, between representatives of the UN and representatives of the belligerent side, whatever side it may be, was it a rule that discussion would take place between officers of the same rank?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Negative. The senior military observer, it had no rank structure. I was a commandant rank, however, I had some colonels from different nationalities under my control.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, thank you for your answer. My question did not relate to internal matters. Was it usual that the UN -- the forces of the UN would have contacts with -- contacts with the belligerent side of this same rank? And I am referring here to protocol, to the usages in practice in the protocol sense.

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: No. At different team sites, it would be the team leader who would be making a protest to the local commander. Rank did not enter into protocol with the UN military observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, are you trying to tell me that perhaps a lieutenant could discuss with a general, discuss matters with a general?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: It is possible. Highly unlikely, but it is possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Why "highly improbable"?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: It would be highly improbable that a lieutenant would be in a position that he would have to discuss items with a general.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, as far as you know, do you think that given the situation on the ground, that a general, a corps commander, would accept to discuss with -- matters with a lieutenant?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: It depended -- it depended on the appointment the lieutenant had at the particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Commandant. You spent about four months in Sarajevo. I would like to ask you a series of questions and to which I would like you to answer by "yes" or "no" because they call for such answers, "yes" or "no." Commandant, do you know what was and where was -- what was Zetra and where it was located?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: "Do you know what was and where was..." Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What was Zetra. Z-e-t-r-a, Zetra?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You don't know where it was located, consequently?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Zetra doesn't ring a bell to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Commandant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to assist you, would it be possible, if you would have similar questions, to ask one general question to the witness and ask him to respond, for example, in the positive, if he knows anything about it; and if you get no response, that it is in the negative. That might be very efficient. It is just a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am -- of course, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you know, Witness, where Zica was?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Can you spell it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Z-i "c" with an accent "a".

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Commandant, could you please tell me if you know how many brigades were located in Sarajevo during your stay there, brigades, 1st Corps of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can you tell me or you do not know?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I cannot recollect. It was ten years ago. I cannot recollect. I have been on three different missions since that mission, and I just don't recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Commandant, have you prepared this testimony with the representatives of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Have you re-read your statement?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did that refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Commandant, do you know how many brigades or -- were located in Sarajevo at the time?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: No, I do not recollect. I don't think in my statement I mentioned a number of brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No, that is true, you did not mention the number. Therefore, Commandant, is it true that you cannot tell us either how many commandments of posts, command and control posts of the battalions, not the brigades? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you say it is correct, that means, "I cannot tell you." Is that what it means?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Commandant, the same -- the same applies to the command post of the companies?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: We have testimony that speak of the existence of mobile military targets. The question is: Have you ever seen such mobile military objectives or targets in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Commandant, were you aware of the fact that there were such military objectives in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us what these objectives were?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I heard that there were one or two mobile mortar platforms within Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Commandant, what are you calling "mortar platforms" and what were their calibres?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: What I am calling is a vehicle with mortars mounted on the back of the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You are saying "mortars." Are you referring to several mortars, a large number of mortars?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I am referring to a vehicle with a mortar or mortars mounted on the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Commandant. Commandant, no information about the calibre of those heavy weapon?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: No, I had no information on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Commandant, where did you get your information from regarding these mobile military objectives?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: It had been said to me that these were being used in Sarajevo. I cannot remember who said it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: If I tell you that that information comes from the information service, would you say that this was acceptable?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: What information service are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Well, it is a question of translation. "Secret service" is what I had wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I am not aware of any secret service in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know of any other mobile targets? We are referring here to vehicles, private vehicles, passenger cars, that could be used for transporting mortars.

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I did not know of any. I didn't know of any particular ones during my time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Commandant, do you know whether the forces of Sarajevo or the BH army, whether they had tanks, and if so, how many?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I know they had some tanks because at the time these tanks were kept in a compound and if the tanks -- I believe there were only a few, maybe two or three, and if these tanks were not in the compound when our UNMOs visited, they reported it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Consequently, General, you are saying that these tanks could move and that they actually moved?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That if they were not in the compound, obviously, they had moved in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I apologise for calling you "General," but you didn't react, but I apologise anyway. Have you, yourself, seen them open fire?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Commandant, do you know whether the -- if the forces of the BH army had the following weapons: Mortar batteries of 120 millimetres?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I couldn't definitely say. I didn't observe the weapons. However, if our UNMOs reported that there had been outgoing fire of 120-millimetre mortars, then they had those. They had those mortars if our UNMOs reported this fire. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But as far as you know personally, you do not know?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: All right. But do you know whether there were such weapons?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I really don't remember. If -- there are plenty written reports during the UNMOs' time. If they reported outgoing 120-millimetre mortars, then the Bosnian army had these weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, if I understood you correctly -- I understood you correctly, but your knowledge of the reports that existed are not perhaps those that we have in this Chamber. That is why I am saying, "as far as you know," not whether you have seen them. Whether the Muslim forces had these 120-millimetre weapons, if so, answer, yes; if not, no.

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I really cannot answer that question. I have answered it already, saying that if we reported 120-millimetre mortars outgoing fire, which there is plenty evidence I am sure of, then they had --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, Commandant I'll interrupt you. Thank you. I think I have your answer. Commandant, the same question for 80-millimetre mortars: Do you remember anything about that? 82 millimetres, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: We had a reporting system, and if those weapons were there, the outgoing fire would have been reported and the number of rounds that were fired. I -- the different types of mortars, I couldn't be sure in my memory at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Let's forget about the mortars since you can't remember about that, and I understand you. Could you reply to the same question but with regard to what are called Howitzers? 105 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I regret to say that I have to give the same answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I accept that answer, Commandant, thank you. Commandant, if I ask you about the Kacusas, what we call multiple rocket launchers, would the answer be the same?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: No, it wouldn't be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I cannot remember Kacusas as such being fired from the Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Commandant, I would like to ask you the same question with regard to the triple-A guns, the anti-aircraft guns.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Defence please repeat the calibres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: From 30 to 12.7 millimetres. It seems we have a problem with interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It might not have been a translation problem, but you pronounced the calibres quite quickly. It now reads on the transcript "from 30 to 12.7 millimetres."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the question is about anti-aircraft guns from 30 to 12.7 millimetres, Mr. O'Keeffe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that these weapons were in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer, Commandant. Sir, do you know whether the forces in Sarajevo had any sniper units, too?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I know that there was sniping being carried out from inside the city, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So the incidents -- these would be incidents that caused loss of life, wounded people, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I cannot remember specific incidents, but I was aware that there was sniping being carried out from inside the city, if I can refer to it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: These sniper shots came from the city and did they target people in the city as well?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: My UNMOs would have reported sniping being carried on in certain areas and those reports would have been sent to our headquarters. I would not be referring to particular sniping incidents. I would be looking at the overall view of how the sniping -- of how much sniping was being carried on at a particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, Commandant. So I will ask you this question in a general manner: Do you know whether in this global view of the things that you had, and you have mentioned about the existence of snipers, sniper shots coming from within the city, do you know whether there were any cases of shots from -- coming from the city and directed at the city?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: No, I don't know of any incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Commandant, do you know where the front lines were located?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I didn't know exactly but we had our map, and our maps were drawn which indicated the front line at the time. And I passed through the front line every time I went to Lukavica. And the front lines, as we saw them, changed a little quite frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Commandant, during your stay, were you aware of the fact that a tunnel was being dug under the airport tarmac?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware. Without it having been confirmed, I believed that there was a tunnel being dug under the tarmac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, a while ago you mentioned the shelling of Sarajevo. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: What particular shelling of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You spoke in general terms about shelling and I think that you mentioned the shelling of an observation post in the centre of Sarajevo. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I mentioned the -- an explosion at one of our observation posts, but this was a tank round that hit the observation post.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. With regard to this incident, could you remind us of the date of this incident?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: No, but I am sure it is in the records somewhere, but I do not have a record of this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, with regard to this particular incident, could you confirm that at the time of the explosion that you mentioned, operations were in progress, that is to say, there was fighting in the surroundings of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes, there was an attack being carried out at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. When you say, "an attack," if that comes from a commandant, if a commandant talks about an attack, it is not just a simple skirmish; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, a while ago, you said that civilian zones were shelled. You mentioned this in general terms. Do you remember talking about this?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I don't think I remember civilians. I didn't say "civilian zones" at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, Commandant. So civilian zones were never shelled in Sarajevo, according to you?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I never mentioned civilian zones. To me --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Commandant, I will ask you the following question: In your opinion, were civilian zones in Sarajevo shelled?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes, civilian zones in Sarajevo were shelled, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Commandant, first of all, I will put to you the following question: When you insist that there was shelling, how do you define what would be a civilian zone in Sarajevo and what would not be a civilian zone in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Civilians, what I am referring to is basically a non-military target, that it was areas -- areas where normal life was going on, and I did not believe that there was military activities in those areas justifying the shelling that was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, Commandant. You used the terms, you said, "I don't think so," but what are the means, or what were the means, of being certain that there were no military targets, mobile military targets, when this shelling took place?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: When our monitors were observing, they reported on incoming rounds landing in particular areas. And they reported to me that there was no military activity, to their knowledge, going on in these particular areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Commandant, if we agree that there were military targets which existed, how can one be absolutely certain that in an area that was shelled which you say was a civilian area, how can one be certain that there wasn't a mobile military target there, whatever the nature of this target? And I am asking how can one be certain of this.

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: It depends on what you consider a military target. Because of the fact one person with a pistol is carrying a pistol and you say that this person is a military target, or one small vehicle has one -- you believe to have one mortar in it, this does not justify firing 1.55 -- 155 ^ shells, numerous 155 shells into a particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Commandant, what did you know about the uniforms that were worn by the BH army at the time of your stay?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Commandant, are you telling me that you didn't know whether the army wore uniforms or what sort of uniforms they had?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: No, I am not saying that. But I did not pay a particular interest to the uniforms that -- uniforms in the city at that particular time. I was very much more interested in meeting people who had influence and who could do something about the crisis situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Commandant, in your own mind, you gave us a definition of civilian zones. Would you agree with me in saying that the Presidency could be described as a military target?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't. I wouldn't consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Is it exact, is it true to say that the Presidency was the abode of the supreme commander of the army?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: As far as I knew, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Commandant, a building in which the supreme commander is located is, in your opinion, not a military target?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Not as far as this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Commandant, I didn't mention a ceasefire, never mentioned a ceasefire. Please answer my question. Don't you consider that the place where the supreme chief of the army is staying, do you think that this is not a military target? I would like things to be clear. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes, it would be a military target.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much for this answer. Commandant, I would like to put the same question to you for vital, important telecommunications centres.

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes, I would say it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, I would like to ask you the same question with regard to important communication centres, and by that I mean the ground centres, both the road networks and the railway network.

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes, I would have to agree, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Than you. Commandant, is it true that command posts, what is usually called command and control posts, are these what we could call legitimate military targets?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, is it true that the operational means, military operational Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. equipment, that this, too, is a legitimate military target?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Sorry, can you -- can you say that again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When I say, "military operational equipment," I am talking about mobile equipment such as tanks, transporters, other mobile operational equipment that is used by an army.

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, groups of soldiers going into operation, in your opinion, are such groups legitimate military targets?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, if many soldiers in Sarajevo did not have regular uniforms, how could military observers of the UN categorically exclude the presence of such groups when there was shelling, the presence of such groups going into operation but people who didn't wear or who weren't wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Of course, the UN military observers couldn't categorically exclude what as -- from my experience, you are trying to say that every person in Sarajevo was --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No, sir, I have to interrupt you. I can't allow that. I can't allow you to interpret what I said. I am just asking you a question, that's all. If there is something that categorically allowed UN officers to exclude this possibility, say so. If not, say so as well.

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Naturally, categorically, they couldn't say this, but in their experience, they would be able to say it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. You say that on the basis of experience, they could have known that. How could they have known whether a group of 10, 15 or 20 people passed through there, how could they have known that if there was no way of distinguishing these men from the remainder of the population? How would this have been possible for them to know?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Basically, this would -- they would rely on their experience and training, making these observations.
