utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, if a troop is present just before a shell and then disappear into thin air, how can UN observers be aware of this fact? There is such thing as experience but, technically speaking, how could they have known this?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: If they didn't observe it, they wouldn't have known it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. Commandant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether you would change to another subject, you said you would split up the time between you and Ms. Pilipovic. I just noticed that you took already more than the examination-in-chief, so I don't know what there is still to be split up. On the other hand, I also noticed that the examination-in-chief was very brief compared to what was indicated before. But I would like to have an indication of you now about the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have a few questions that have to do with humanitarian issues, a cassette which takes 2 minutes and 25 seconds, and then a few brief questions that will be put by Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ten minutes, would that be fair? I am asking you that because I notice now and then that if a certain limited time is given to you, that the efficiency raises greatly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you say to me -- are you speaking to me personally? Is it the "vous" which is singular in French or the "vous" which is plural?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... to use the English language; it makes no distinction. If 10 minutes would not be enough -- would 10 minutes for you be enough, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ten minutes for me, that would be necessary and sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I expect that Ms. Pilipovic takes over at quarter past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Commandant, a while ago, you spoke about brigades. Do you know whether at that time there was a brigade, a Mujahedin Brigade in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: No, I didn't know of --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Do you know whether there was a brigade which consisted also of women?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, you said that one of the missions of the UN observers was to verify the transport of humanitarian aid; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: No, it was to assist in the humanitarian aid convoys as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. So to assist the convoys. Were there UNHCR convoys among these convoys?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I am aware, yes, there were UNHCR convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, is it true to say that in the statement that we referred to earlier on that you made a few years ago, is it true to say that you told the Serbs that you would do everything you could to ensure that humanitarian convoys were also sent over to the Serbians to solve problems of poverty and misfortune?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I put the UNHCR in contact with people on the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that this would be a good time to have a look at the cassette. I hope that we won't have any problems with showing it because I know that, in the past, we have had such problems. So I would just like to say that I hope there won't be any problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see what happens when we ask the technical booth to play the video. But perhaps first, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in his absence, Mr. Ierace has reviewed the videotape and has e-mailed me with respect to the tape. I would like to query Mr. Piletta-Zanin whether he is planning on having the audio portion of the tape played as well, or simply the video?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both, both.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution would object to the audio portion of the tape being played, for reasons which I can elaborate on, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would it be wise to do it in the presence of the witness or should we do it in the absence of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that it be done in the absence of the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. O'Keeffe, since there is a certain objection against what is going to be played to you, we would rather discuss it in your absence. I hope you don't mind, and I hope you do understand. So, Mr. Usher, would you please escort Mr. O'Keeffe out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, it appears from the information I received via e-mail that the videotape is a Bosnian Serb television report having to do with humanitarian aid convoys. It appears to be a news report, and it includes a voice-over and an interview of someone in Serbian. And the reason we would object to that would be a couple of reasons, first of all, whether or not this witness would have seen this news report. I believe, if this witness were to be asked, he would inform the Trial Chamber that he does not in fact speak, nor understand, the Serbian language. So for us, our position would be that the audio that is contained on this news report would have little or no probative value, nor relevance to the proceedings. If the intent is simply to show him the video of what is contained on the videotape and to ask him if he has seen these things or if he can comment or elaborate on them, we have no objection. But with respect to playing a news report in a language that the witness doesn't understand, would seem, to the Prosecution, to have little or no probative value and no relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from whether there is a translation available for the Bench and for the Prosecution to understand what -- you prepared it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is in fact the text, the entire text, of what is said on that tape, and what we suggest is that we provide the booths with the text so that they can verify what is said and perhaps translate what is said on the tape. A cassette without text seems to be a little truncated. I think there are important translations here. Now I have to admit that I failed to do so, I omitted it, because I thought that the translation could be done immediately in the Office of the Prosecutor. They have a lot of translators there

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...unfortunate that you had a translation prepared. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the Chamber finds that you should first provide now the translation to the Prosecution, that the Prosecution is in a position just to read what is said. It cannot be more than two minutes, so it cannot be a very long text. As far as we understand, Mr. Ierace, you have at least seen the video. You will now be provided by a written translation of the text, and not show it before the Prosecution has had an opportunity to at least to read what text is used in the video. Then we will see -- after they have had an opportunity to do so, we will see whether we could proceed in playing the video to the witness or whatever could happen. Perhaps, in order to give some time, we could have an early break since we might not end very late today. So if we would take our relatively short break now for 20 minutes, that would mean that we would resume at 25 minutes to 6.00. Then, Mr. Ierace, you will have an opportunity to read the text and confer with Mr. Mundis, and then we could continue afterward.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. On page 49, line 2 of the transcript, it is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...a translation had been prepared so that we can at least proceed at this very moment and we are not dependent on provisional translations to be made. We will adjourn for 20 minutes. Could please Mr. O'Keeffe be informed? I don't know who is taking care. Could you please, Mr. Usher, inform Mr. O'Keeffe that we take the opportunity to have a break until 5 minutes past -- no, I have to say 25 minutes to 6.00. --- Break taken at 5.15 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, I see you are on your feet so I take it that you have read the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I have, Mr. President, and I have made some copies of the English transcript which Mr. Piletta-Zanin gave me, if you or the other members of the Bench wish a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it depends on if the video will be played. I think the first ones who need a copy are the interpreters. If they have a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. copy, I might do without, but if there are any other copies, the Chamber would be glad to have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, I will hand over the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has copies. They can make them available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to have for the Chamber four copies, two of the Defence and two of the Prosecution. May I take it that the interpreters' booth have been provided with copies? Yes. Two more copies for the Prosecution. Thank you. Is there anything else you would like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I would like to amplify my objection to not only the playing of the audio, but more fundamentally, the playing of the video altogether. Firstly, having regard to the transcript, it is confirmed that this tape purports to be a copy of a television, presumably, news transmission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- in relation to an incident at Ilidza, undated - which is important - where apparently arms in the form of ammunition were smuggled into -- attempted to be smuggled into Sarajevo from Split. Now that is according to the transcript. My first point is that given it is undated, it is therefore entirely unclear whether this is an incident which took place during the time that the witness was in Sarajevo. My second point is that assuming it is an incident which occurred during the tenure of the witness in Sarajevo, the appropriate course is simply to put to the witness: Are you aware of an incident when ammunition was discovered, concealed within a humanitarian aid shipment? If the witness says he is not, then that is the end of the matter. Showing the video then has no relevance at all. Thirdly, in relation to the voice-over, once you have had an opportunity to read the transcript, it will become apparent that it contains the opinions of someone, presumably the reporter or whoever wrote the text, beyond that, a comment from herself and a person whom she interviewed who purported to be some sort of security officer or police officer. Mr. President, there is a more fundamental objection. What is the relevance of this to the Defence case? Is the Defence saying that ammunition was smuggled into Sarajevo in United Nations' convoys or other humanitarian aid convoys and, therefore, the United Nations' vehicles or humanitarian aid vehicles or United Nations personnel became legitimate military targets? This needs to be spelled out. If that is not what the Defence is saying, then in what way is this relevant, assuming that it is true. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's first ask Mr. Piletta-Zanin what he seeks to establish by showing this video to the witness and ask the witness questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I would agree with Mr. Ierace concerning the audio part and when he says that it expresses the opinion of a journalist. But, since it is something that we have re-copied, we wish to re-copy it in its entirety, both audio and the images, so as not to be blamed for concealing something. What we wish to seek to establish is that, very often, the Prosecution indicates that there may have been problems with vehicles which were of an interest to the UN forces. This, we could see yesterday. Now, whatever the decision may be, and without wishing to say that this or that object bearing the UN designation, the Defence nevertheless wishes to show that there may have been some case of nervousness among some, and that at levels inferior to General Galic, and there may have been aggressive action. And this is something that we have to establish during the general proceedings because the Prosecution has mentioned that the witness has said certain things, and we wish to strike a balance that there have been serious cases where the staff, the personnel that the tape deals with, was involved in trafficking of arms, and I think we should not omit mentioning this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...what divides you and Mr. Ierace at this time is what the truth is. Of course, it cannot be circumvented. I think -- but I am just trying to understand the positions of the parties. I didn't hear Mr. Ierace say that no evidence should be produced in respect of, as you called it, very serious events which might have invoked certain reactions, without saying that UN personnel was ever attacked. I think what we are dealing with is the way of introducing such evidence. It might be that the witness knows something about it. I have no idea. But do I understand you well, Mr. Ierace, that you are saying, well, produce this evidence but not through a witness who might not know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, subject to the issue of relevance. But the threshold question, Mr. President, if you are of the view that it does have relevance, is firstly, to enquire of the Defence what is the evidence that this incident happened in the period that Mr. O'Keeffe was in Sarajevo. Or at least, if my friend doesn't know that, to simply ask the witness whether he is aware of such an incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Could I just add one further point, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What I seek is nothing more than what the Prosecution has committed itself to. You will recall that during my opening, we showed a collage of video clips. The evidence will be in relation to those video clips from Mr. Lesic, Zoran Lesic, that most of those clips came from television stations, and you will recall that there were no voice-overs from commentators on those clips. All of those voice-overs- there were some initially- were cleaned off because, clearly, what a commentator says is not evidence. And so I merely seek to hold the Defence to what the Prosecution regards as the proper aspects of such sources of such material. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps to make one observation, because the Chamber has given it some thought as well. The opinion of journalists is, of course -- is very dangerous, especially in a jury trial, for professional judges who have seen television on from when it started to appear in our houses. And I am still the youngest. And whoever read newspapers since they could read. Is not perhaps that -- it is not that fragile, I would say, in a Bench trial as it is in a jury trial. I hope that you will understand that so that we might be a bit more liberal on that issue. Could you inform us, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, of the dates of the events, whether this was within the period of --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, I will ask the question -- I ask the question about the date to Madam Pilipovic, but as a point of relevance, I would like to state the following: The pictures that we will see will be the pictures that have to do with arms trafficking. And we can see at a certain moment the ammunition that was concealed there. And this witness stated that he could not remember exactly what sort of weapons the BH army had during his stay there, and I am almost sure that if we show, through this video, the ammunition and we show it to this military person, he can say it will be 12.7 calibre millimetres. We can conclude that if such ammunition is delivered, it is delivered to be used and not to be stashed away. As regards the date, I will ask about it. Mr. President, as you have noted, where we had decided to use it on this part, we believe it to be a date that corresponds to the date of this stay of the witness in Sarajevo. We don't have the information here and now. We can look for them later on but, at any rate, since the Defence is indicating this, that these are events that have reoccurred, we wanted to ask the witness to find out whether he was aware of the fact that such problems were noticed and had indeed occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, nothing that my learned colleague has said has been responsive to the issues that I have raised. Most significantly, it is not suggested by the Defence that Mr. O'Keeffe was present when this convoy was allegedly found to contain ammunition on its way on a route destined to Sarajevo. There is no reason why the course that I have proposed should not be adopted. It is the proper course. The witness should simply be asked if he is aware of such an incident, and that is assuming that it has some probative value. And if he is not, that is the end of it, because if he is not, what possible probative value is there in playing him a series of images of an incident of which he has no awareness? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: What the Trial Chamber confirms, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, did I hear you saying that it is not your intention to say that the UN vehicles are a legitimate military target? You said that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be very clear. The Defence has never said or nor has the intention of saying that, in its view, that the UN troops were a legitimate military target. I will check on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...transcript is not --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your observation, sir, but what I will say is that it was not definitely. I hope it's clear. Thanks very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This gives the opportunity to just to read the transcript of the last one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I said, "are not" again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber finds it proper to start, at least, with a question to the witness, whether he knows about this incident or these kind of incidents. Once we know the answer to that question, then of course we have to see what the next step will be. May I make one observation, Mr. Piletta-Zanin? Where you at least suggested several times that what was on the video was more or less an undeniable fact, this Chamber never would assume on the mere basis of looking at the video that it was an undeniable fact what was shown on the video. This Chamber has also seen movies for some 50 years. But, of course, a lot of things are true which is shown on videos, but just in order to make clear what the position of the Chamber will be anyhow, that whatever we see on a video, we will have to establish whether this video reflects the truth or does not reflect the truth. That is not only for videos of the Defence but is similarly true for whatever video is shown by the Prosecution. So, then, please could Mr. O'Keeffe be brought into the courtroom again, and would you start with the question indicated?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence hopes not to practice excessively anamorphose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Our witness is now and then suffering under Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. procedural issues we deal with in their absence, but we now continue. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will ask the question, but I want to repeat this for the transcript. "Anamorphose," for the English transcript, in order to clarify matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Commandant, good day again. I would like to ask you the following question: While you were in Sarajevo, did you hear any protests relating to the fact that one or the other of the warring factions -- did you hear any protests coming from one or the other of the warring factions?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that not a bit -- very unspecific, one of the parties protesting?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: About what, for example?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand in general, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever hear the Serb party involved in the conflict complaining about the existence of certain illegitimate trafficking, for example, of weapons in the direction of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I don't remember any formal protest that was made by the Serbian side in relation to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I appreciate your answer, sir, but it is necessary to be very precise. You say you don't remember any formal complaints. I am not referring to formal complaints, but did you ever hear, and I don't mean a formal complaint, any protest of a general nature that the Serbian side might have made with this respect, in this respect?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: With regard to what specific --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: For example, with regard to the trafficking or illegal importing of arms into Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I heard of complaints made about people and weapons being brought in, in relation to the tunnel in the airport situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can I stop you here, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, given this answer, may I show the cassette or do I have to continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, because it wasn't very specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, did you hear whether, apart from imports that came through the tunnel, were there any other imports, were any other weapons transported, brought in to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I didn't hear of any rumours or hear of rumours or it wasn't -- it was not reported to me of any such situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, you never heard anyone mentioning the Operation Oxygen?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: No, definitely not. I never heard of that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, you never heard the Containers Operation being referred to?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean by "Containers Operation."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, it is the name. It is a code. It is the name of an operation which was called "Containers."

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: No, I never heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, have you ever heard a rumour or a complaint made by the Serbian party according to which certain UNHCR vehicles were allegedly used to take to the city of Sarajevo things that were not humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: No, I did not. Sorry, could I -- Your Honour, I am getting no picture on my screen as regard to questions at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and I notice that you appreciate to, apart from hearing, also to read what is written. It does appear now on your screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. President, given that this witness has no knowledge of this transport of weapons above ground but only knowledge of transport of weapons under ground, I don't think it is necessary to show him the cassette. But Ms. Pilipovic has a few questions to ask within the period of time that has been given to her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hope you do not misunderstand the position of the Chamber, that this would be an, under all circumstances, irrelevant video of not containing aspects of the conflicts that might be important for the Defence to produce. It is just the technical issues we are just dealing with at this moment, and I just hope that there is no misunderstanding about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence takes into account your remark. We understand it. I don't think you have misunderstood me, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. O'Keeffe. Mr. O'Keeffe, you told us and confirmed that you had given a statement to investigators of the Prosecution and that you read that statement and refreshed your memory with regard to the period during which you were in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. O'Keeffe, I will remind you of something on page 6 of your statement. You spoke about the tactics used by the Bosnians and you called this the mosquito tactics. Do you remember saying this?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. O'Keeffe, could you clarify this matter for us. When you mentioned the mosquito tactics, what did you mean by that? What sort of tactics are involved?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: It means where a small force is operating against a big force, that they make an attack which is really not an attack to overcome the big force but it irritates the larger force. That is what I mean by a "mosquito attack."

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. O'Keeffe, would you agree that in situations where such tactics are employed, it is difficult to know what the real and final objective of such tactics is?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes, it would be difficult, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that in such a situation, the stronger side, as you say, was not in a position, was not able to know, the real and final objective of such tactics?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes, that would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. O'Keeffe, in your opinion, is it the legitimate right of the side that is attacked to defend itself and use all the means it has at its disposal to do so?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes, to defend itself, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Keeffe. On page 6, you also said that it was very difficult at night to determine whether shots were coming from weapons from one kilometre or from further away; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that in such cases the UN observers were not able to be precise, they might have made random estimates as to where the shell came from?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: It would have depended again on the situation at the particular time. I think I was referring to shelling that the observers were not close to.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. O'Keeffe, can you tell us whether the -- whether in Sarajevo and its surroundings was such that it might have not been possible for the observers to be precise? And I am thinking in particular of fog.

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I had impressed on my observers that if they had ever any doubt, that they should not report items, that they should be very definite in their reporting.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. O'Keeffe, on page 7 of your statement you said, and I shall read this to you, it is just one line: "The Bosnians had the entire world press on their side so that these reprisals were sometimes used in order to create an unfavourable image of the Serbs." Is that something that you stated?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. O'Keeffe, in your opinion, did the reports from UN observers also contribute to portraying the Serbs in a negative light?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes, the reports would have contributed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: One question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Commandant O'Keeffe, if a captain was the senior officer, senior UNMO officer, on the Lima side at Lukavica barracks, would that captain occasionally be called upon to meet with the corps commander as part of his duties, such as to present a protest or lodge a complaint?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes, it would have been part of his duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask you if you could clarify a matter which appears in your statement. In your statement you mentioned the issue, the nature of the protest that you lodged with regard to -- with regard to a shelling, and I quote you: [In English] "That I could not understand to be military targets." [Interpretation] And you mentioned that as a response you received the following response, and I quote: [In English] "He was going to make this area safe for his children's children." This reply, was it in response to your complaint, to your protest, or was it a sentence in the course of your conversation, as far as you can remember, to the best of your recollection of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: In my recollection, it was in a conversation at the end of the meeting, when I asked a question like, "What do you really want in this crisis?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Colonel O'Keeffe, I also have a question for you. You have told us about several meetings you had with General Galic. The first meeting you described, which was not your first meeting - that was, at least, not when you first met General Galic - was about the Papa 5 having been fired at. You told us that, apart from this specific issue, the normal protests about the situation were communicated. You then explained to us that the normal protest was about sniping, shelling, not specifically to Papa 5. When you told us about later meetings with General Galic, you said that you do not remember specific subjects being discussed during these meetings. Would that mean that it is not in your recollection what the specific reasons for your visits were or the specific subjects, or that the, as you called them, the normal protest, I think you said, would not have been discussed during these meetings either? Have you no recollection at all or just not on specific issues other than normal issues?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I really have no recollection of what in particular we discussed at these meetings, that I couldn't refer to any one incident during these meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Normal or particular? None?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: What I am saying is I would have, at these meetings, in the normal course of events, I would have again objected to the sniping, the indiscriminate firing, the breaking of local -- the breaking of ceasefires, items like that that were continuously ongoing every day, with the result that I am not able to remember, you know, any specific one to be brought up at one particular time. It would have been normal for me to say, "Well, why don't you stop the sniping?" "Why don't you stop the shelling?" "Why won't you let the convoys through?" "Why won't you let the airplanes come in?" These are the types of things I would have been saying. What I cannot remember -- you know, I would have been doing this so frequently that I cannot refer to any specific one at any particular time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand you well that you said these were the kind of subjects that we discussed also during the other meetings, but whether on the 5th or the 6th or the 7th, we mentioned sniping or we didn't mention sniping specifically, I've got no -- but sniping and shelling have been discussed at one or more of these other meetings; is that how I am to understand you?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That makes it clearer for me. Commandant O'Keeffe, you have answered all the questions of both parties and of the Bench. I thank you very much for having come to The Hague and giving your testimony in this Court. Ms. Pilipovic, would you -- Ms. Pilipovic knows that --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that in speaking these words, that the witness will usually be out of the courtroom in one or two minutes. So since she stands, I will first give her the opportunity to interrupt me. Yes, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Mr. O'Keeffe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would have another question?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a bit unusual. Is there any reason, Ms. Pilipovic, or you have just have one question, five questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will be very brief. The questions have to do with the meeting, and since during the examination-in-chief the Prosecution didn't ask these questions, the Defence thought that it was not necessary to put these questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. O'Keeffe, could you tell us how long these meetings lasted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I first just explain, usually if the Bench has raised a certain issue, then the parties have an additional opportunity to ask additional questions to these questions. Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't recall how long these meetings took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. O'Keeffe, you said that you had mentioned sniping incidents and shelling incidents. Could you please tell us of one meeting, a particular meeting, which you mentioned to General Galic at one of those meetings that you had?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: No, I cannot -- this is what I explained before, and that I cannot specifically say at one particular meeting that I said these things. But during my meetings with him, I would have invariably brought up these items. I am not saying that there was one specific one that I brought it up or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. O'Keeffe, could you tell us what else you spoke about at these meetings, apart from this subject?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I cannot remember any other items that we discussed at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: One more question, Mr. O'Keeffe: When, as you said, you went to the meetings, whether formal or informal, could you tell us whether you had a translator, an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: I do not think so. I think that the translator was -- there was a translator provided by General Galic or -- I am not sure, but I think the liaison officers -- liaison officer would have translated from time to time, but I think there was an interpreter there at most meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say, "I think at most of the meetings," do you mean to say that at some of the meetings there was no interpreter?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: No. What I am saying is that, as far as I recollect, a person speaking English was always, naturally enough, at the meeting because I could not understand any other language. So somebody had to interpret or explain to me what was happening at the meeting or what I said. But I cannot specifically say whether it was the liaison officer, another officer or an interpreter. But there was somebody there who translated at the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. O'Keeffe, the translations you would receive from the interpreters who were present there, were the translations always clear and could you always understand them?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. If I had difficulty, I would have asked the question again at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. O'Keeffe, you told us that the first time you had a meeting with Mr. Galic, Mr. Cutler was present with you; is that correct, during the transfer of duties? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DONOUGH EMANUEL ^ O'KEEFFE
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. O'Keeffe, I am going to show you Mr. Cutler's statement which he gave to the investigators of the Prosecutor on the 13th of January, 1997, and 18th of March, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution will object first of all in showing the statement, but as a more general proposition, we would object that this has gone beyond the scope of questions put to the witness from the Bench. And these would have been properly -- could have been properly asked of the witness following the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is sustained. Is there any other question specifically related -- well, this is already a question you indicated --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- four questions before that that would be your last one. Commandant O'Keeffe, when I said to you that you answered all the questions of the parties, that was not true, because there were still some questions remaining. But, now you have. Perhaps not all, but all the questions being put to you have been answered by now. May I thank you very much for having come to The Hague, and may I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please escort Mr. O'Keeffe out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, we have no documents to be admitted. That means that we will adjourn until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon. I take it then, Mr. Mundis, that you will start with the examination-in-chief of Mr. Thomas?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
